**Research note: PostgreSQL limits for schema and pool sizing**

I checked each figure against the official PostgreSQL documentation (the "current" pages) in this session.

**Identifier length.** By default, an identifier such as a table or column name can be at most 63 bytes. The build constant `NAMEDATALEN` is 64, and the server uses at most `NAMEDATALEN`-1 bytes of any identifier (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). Longer names are not rejected. They are silently truncated to 63 bytes, so two long names that share a 63-byte prefix will collide. The limit counts bytes, not characters, so multibyte UTF-8 names hit it sooner. The same limit appears on the documentation's limits page (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). It can only be raised by changing `NAMEDATALEN` and recompiling PostgreSQL. That is not an option on managed services, so treat 63 bytes as fixed.

**Columns per table.** A table can have at most 1,600 columns (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). The practical ceiling is lower, because each row has to fit in a single 8192-byte heap page. The documentation's own example is that 1,600 `int` columns (6,400 bytes) fit, but 1,600 `bigint` columns (12,800 bytes) do not. Dropped columns still count toward the 1,600 (same page). A table that is regularly altered can therefore lose headroom over time. In practice you should never be near this limit. A table with hundreds of columns usually signals a modelling problem.

**Default max_connections.** The default is typically 100 (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). The docs add that it "might be less if your kernel settings will not support it", as determined by `initdb` when the cluster is created. The parameter can only be changed at server start, so a change means a restart. Running `SHOW max_connections;` on the target server confirms the actual value. Managed providers often override the default, so check their documentation as well.

**Recommendation.** Keep all table and column names well under 63 bytes, ideally under about 50 and ASCII-only, and design tables with tens of columns rather than approaching 1,600. Size the service's connection pool to fit comfortably within max_connections (100 by default), leaving headroom for admin, migration and monitoring sessions and for other services sharing the server. Consider a pooler such as PgBouncer if you need many client connections.

**Research note: PostgreSQL memory and WAL defaults**

I checked the current official PostgreSQL documentation for the three defaults. The WAL page was the PostgreSQL 18 version.

**work_mem.** The default is 4MB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). This limit applies per sort or hash operation, not per connection. A single complex query can use several multiples of it, so raise it with care.

**shared_buffers.** The default is typically 128MB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The docs add that it might be less if your kernel settings can't support it, as determined during initdb. Check `SHOW shared_buffers;` on the fresh install rather than assuming 128MB.

**max_wal_size.** The default is 1GB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). It is a soft limit on how much WAL can accumulate between automatic checkpoints. The same page gives min_wal_size a default of 80MB.

**Recommendation.** Treat all three as conservative starting points. Raise shared_buffers and max_wal_size for a real workload, which reduces checkpoint frequency, and raise work_mem gradually, ideally per role or per session. Change one setting at a time and measure.

DuckDB's default memory limit is 80% of RAM, SQLite's maximum database file is 281 TB, and MERGE first shipped in PostgreSQL 15.

**Research note: analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL, and MERGE on PG 15**

**DuckDB memory.** DuckDB's configuration reference lists `memory_limit` (alias `max_memory`) with a default of 80% of system RAM (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html). The older stable URL I tried first only redirected to this page. On a shared host, the Postgres server and DuckDB would both claim most of the memory. I would set the limit explicitly, for example `SET memory_limit='4GB'`, instead of relying on the default. DuckDB can spill to disk, but a sensible cap still avoids contention with Postgres.

**SQLite size.** The SQLite "Implementation Limits" page says the maximum database file is 4294967294 pages. At the maximum page size of 65536 bytes, that is about 281 terabytes (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). At the default 4096-byte page size, the limit is about 17.5 TB. The page also says the upper bound is untested. In practice the filesystem or disk will limit you long before SQLite does. Size is not what separates these two options for a side-store. SQLite is a row-oriented engine tuned for transactional work. DuckDB is columnar and vectorised, which suits scans and aggregations.

**MERGE on PostgreSQL 15.** The PostgreSQL 15 release notes list "Add SQL `MERGE` command to adjust one table to match another" under Utility Commands (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/). The PG 15 manual page documents MERGE as a single statement that can conditionally INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE rows (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-merge.html). That manual page does not say which version introduced the command. The release notes are what establish PostgreSQL 15 as the first major version with MERGE. So MERGE is available on PG 15 and later, but not on 14 or earlier. The release notes describe it as similar to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` but more batch-oriented.

**Recommendation.** Choose DuckDB for the analytics side-store, because its columnar engine fits aggregation-heavy queries, and cap its memory so it does not compete with Postgres. Use MERGE on PostgreSQL 15 for batch upserts into the operational tables, and fall back to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` only if you must support PG 14 or earlier.

**Research note: TLS version, DNS label length and HTTP 418**

**1. TLS 1.3.** TLS 1.3 was specified in RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", published in August 2018 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). That page now marks RFC 8446 as obsolete. Its replacement is RFC 9846, a Proposed Standard dated July 2026 with the same title, which states that it "obsoletes RFC 8446, which specified TLS 1.3" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846). It is a minor, backward-compatible update that keeps the version number. It also obsoletes the TLS 1.2 specification, RFC 5246, and adds new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations. A guideline should therefore cite RFC 9846 as the current specification and mention RFC 8446 only as the original one. The question's literal answer is 8446, but 9846 is the current reference.

**2. DNS label length.** A single DNS label is limited to 63 octets. RFC 1035 says "Labels must be 63 characters or less" in section 2.3.1 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). The same RFC limits a whole domain name to 255 octets, counting the length bytes, in section 3.1 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). The 255 limit is a separate rule, so a guideline should state both.

**3. HTTP 418.** The status code "418 I'm a teapot" is defined in RFC 2324, the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0). It reads: "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code '418 I'm a teapot'" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). The RFC is dated 1 April 1998 and is an April Fools' joke, though it carries the Informational status. It is not part of the HTTP standard. I tried to confirm 418's current status in RFC 9110 but the fetched excerpt did not reach the status code section, so I can't say from this session how that RFC treats 418.

**Recommendation.** Cite RFC 9846 (with RFC 8446 noted as its predecessor) for TLS 1.3, and require host-name validation to enforce both the 63-octet label limit and the 255-octet name limit. Don't use 418 for real application errors. Treat it as a joke code and pick a standard 4xx code instead.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 8446 (original TLS 1.3; obsoleted by RFC 9846)", "2": "63 octets", "3": "418, RFC 2324"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324"]}}

**Research note: limits for the deploy runbook**

**Lambda timeout.** A single Lambda invocation can be configured for at most 900 seconds (15 minutes). The default is 3 seconds, adjustable in 1-second steps (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The same page says Lambda Managed Instances allow up to 5,400 seconds for asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations. That exception doesn't apply to standard functions, so I'd plan on 900 seconds.

**Kubernetes grace period.** A Pod is given 30 seconds to terminate gracefully by default (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). The page quotes this sentence but doesn't tie it to a field name in the part I read. The `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is the usual way to override it, and the same page mentions that field. I did not read a page that explicitly says the field defaults to 30. The kubelet sends SIGTERM when termination starts and SIGKILL once the grace period runs out.

**Docker docker0 subnet.** The default bridge network uses 172.17.0.0/16 (source: https://docs.nebius.com/compute/virtual-machines/docker-subnet-conflict). This is a vendor page, not Docker's own documentation. Docker's bridge driver page (https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/) only shows a container on 172.17.0.2 in an example and doesn't state the subnet. Docker's daemon and firewall pages say nothing about it either. The Nebius page also notes that this range can collide with VMs on the same private range. The `bip` key in `daemon.json` moves docker0 to another subnet.

**Recommendation.** Set the function timeout and the Pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` explicitly, and make the shutdown handler finish well inside the shorter of the two limits. Check that 172.17.0.0/16 doesn't overlap your VPC or office ranges, and set `bip` if it does.

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

**Vitest per-test timeout.** Vitest's `testTimeout` option defaults to 5,000 ms in Node. If `browser.enabled` is true, the default is 15,000 ms (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout).

**Linux kernel and Rust.** Linux 6.1 was the first mainline release with Rust support. The KernelNewbies page for that release says "This release adds support for the Rust programming language." It describes the support as initial and limited, to be improved in later releases (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). The kernel's own Rust documentation page (https://docs.kernel.org/rust/index.html) did not say which version came first, so the version rests on the KernelNewbies page alone. That is a secondary source, not the kernel tree itself.

**PostgreSQL statement_timeout.** The default is 0, which disables the timeout. Without units, a value is read as milliseconds. The docs also advise against setting it in `postgresql.conf`, since that would affect every session (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html).

**Recommendation.** Keep vitest at 5,000 ms and override it per test or per project only where needed (for example 15,000 ms for browser mode). Set a finite `statement_timeout` per role or per session, not globally, and track the Rust-for-Linux version the team follows against 6.1 as the baseline.

{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms (15000 ms in browser mode)", "2": "Linux 6.1", "3": "0 (disabled)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html"]}}
